subject: jukebox
pitch: A 1950s diner jukebox. A tall rounded arch of glowing coloured tubes in red, amber and teal, chrome trim everywhere, a domed glass window showing a stack of records and the arm that picks them, rows of chrome selection buttons with little title cards, a speaker grille with a starburst pattern, and a coin slot.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the jukebox model structure, reviewing which builder methods and part primitives the SDK offers so I can construct it piece by piece.

I'm also sketching the module's export shape—a default function returning the root with a meta object—and figuring out the chrome trim material using a matte standard material with specific roughness and metalness values.

Since colors are just matte strings with no true metalness, I'm planning to fake chrome using light silver-grey tones with gradient or striped paint for highlights, and glowing tubes using bright saturated colors instead of emissive materials. For the domed glass window, since transparency isn't available, I'm considering building it as an open-fronted lathe shell so the stacked records inside remain visible without needing actual glass opacity.

I'm reconsidering the classic Wurlitzer design instead: a tall arch of glowing colored tubes up top, a domed glass window in the middle showing the record stack and arm, chrome trim throughout, selection buttons with title cards, a starburst speaker grille, and a coin slot.

Now I'm working out the stylized dimensions for the cabinet, roughly 1.55m tall and 0.66m wide, oriented facing forward with the base resting on the ground, and planning to build the body using an extruded side profile along the width axis.

I'm sketching the side silhouette of the cabinet in the z-y plane — a box with a rounded top and sloped front — considering a bevel option for rounded rims versus a simpler boxy geometry for ease of construction.

Now I'm planning the vertical layout of the jukebox front view, thinking through the real Wurlitzer 1015 reference: chrome plinth at the base, speaker grille with starburst above it, chrome trim, and a coin slot on the front-right at waist height, before figuring out where the arched tube bubbler and record-display dome sit higher up.

I'm working out the selection panel layout — deciding between a 2-column rack versus a grid of rows, settling on something like 3 rows of 5 small chrome-capped button cylinders in varied colors (red, amber, teal, cream, chrome) paired with title cards, set against a flat colored front panel plate.

Now I'm moving up to design the arch of glowing tube lighting that frames the domed record window: an upside-down U-shaped sweep of tubing that encloses the dome, inside which I'm planning to place a stack of thin record discs with colored labels and the picker arm.

I'm working out how to build the arch itself using nested concentric semicircular tubes in red, amber, and teal, generated as swept paths of small circular radius along a polyline approximation of the curve, relying on smooth-skin fillets to round the corners so the path reads as a seamless neon loop rather than a jointed shape.

Actually, maybe simpler: three single-colour tubes nested as concentric arches with slightly different radii and z-offsets, spaced enough to avoid overlap. I'm now thinking through the overall composition zones by height — plinth at the base, then the lower front section, working up toward where the glass dome and record window sit within the arch's framing.

For the speaker grille with the starburst pattern, I'm planning to paint it directly onto a rounded rectangular panel using angular ray math — computing the angle from local surface coordinates and checking against a ring pattern to create the sunburst rays, since the extrude surface naturally gives local x,y coordinates centered on the panel origin.

For zone C, the selection panel, I'm laying out three rows of small cylindrical buttons oriented to face forward using the part's directional aim parameter, plus small title card rectangles that I still need to figure out how to render with text.

For title cards, I'm weighing between using a decal projected onto the front panel versus simple textured plane geometry — since planes face +Z by default, that avoids extra rotation logic and seems like the simpler path for the card surfaces.

I realize parts with an `at` position but no bone require a nearest-joint lookup, which fails if no joints exist yet, so I need to create a root joint at the origin before placing any card geometry.

For moving parts like a record picker arm, I could add a child joint with a hinge role, though I'll keep the rig minimal since this is a prop rather than a creature — just enough joints to anchor pieces without overcomplicating things.

Now I'm thinking through the paint sheet setup: with a 2048 texel sheet and roughly 3 square meters of painted surface, the density works out to around 968 texels per meter, which should give crisp detail. I'm deciding which parts get painted gradients versus flat colors — chrome trim is a good candidate for a light-to-dark gradient to fake a metallic streak look, while tubes and stripes get their own paint treatment for visual richness.

Writing custom chrome paint function...

The returned values get baked as sRGB texel data, matching how the colour strings are interpreted elsewhere, so the look stays consistent since normals are evaluated per-texel in model space. Now I'm checking the resource limits — part count, triangle budget, joint count, and flat colour palette size — to make sure this approach stays within bounds.

I'm sketching the cabinet's side profile in meters, defining the plinth, main body, and taper as a set of (z, y) coordinate points to extrude into the shape, keeping the geometry simple while giving it a slight outward flare at the base.

Still refining extrude points...

With the bevel, that front rim will round nicely. Now thinking about color scheme: the cabinet sides are flat big faces I can paint, while the front rim band is the main visible face — classic jukeboxes went cream or oxblood red with chrome trim, so I'm leaning toward a cream-white cabinet body with chrome accents and colorful tube glows (red/amber/teal) rather than matching reds, to keep good contrast against the tubes.

I'm settling on cherry-red lacquer for the lower cabinet body, cream panels for the front selection area, chrome trim throughout, red/amber/teal glowing tubes in the arch, and a dark navy interior behind the dome showing multicolored record labels — this gives enough contrast between the deeper cabinet red and the brighter tube red.

Since one paint function applies across an entire extruded mesh, I'm realizing the cream side panels and front need to share consistent treatment, so I'm using a subtle grain texture blending two close cream tones for the sides while keeping the red lacquer and starburst chrome pattern on the lower speaker grille panel.

For the chrome trim, I'm planning rod or sweep-based bands around the cabinet edges and front window frame to give that classic jukebox metallic outline. Then I start blocking out the front-face zones vertically — plinth at the bottom in chrome, moving upward through the colored panels toward the arch.

Now I'm sketching the cabinet's silhouette profile as a sequence of z,y coordinates, working through the kick bevel, front shoulder, and rounded top — but I realize the dome and tube arch sit higher up near the top shoulder, which conflicts with my current profile, so I need to rethink how the rounded "bubbler" top integrates with the front arch geometry.

I'm restructuring into two sections: a lower cabinet body (y 0 to 1.15) and a separate upper "head" extrude (y 1.15 to 1.62) holding the arch and dome, set back slightly with its own narrower silhouette. For the front face, I'm planning a speaker grille panel with a painted starburst and chrome bezel around y 0.20–0.56, plus a coin slot positioned on the model's right side.

Above that, I'm designing a selection panel with cream plate backing, three rows of five chrome buttons each, and small title cards textured with painted text (like song titles) sitting above each button row.

Settling on 3 rows × 4 columns instead, giving 12 buttons and 12 title cards, each with its own generated SVG texture carrying a unique title string.

I'll draw text in color directly on the SVG rather than relying on tinting, since the part() helper only tints white when texture isn't marked as "coloured." Each card part gets placed with weights derived from its nearest joint on the cabinet frame, same as the buttons.

For the arch, I'm sweeping glowing tubes along a catmull curve in front of the head plane, floating slightly off the surface — treating it as a chrome bezel channel rather than needing physical supports since it's visually anchored to the frame.

For the dome window, I'm thinking of it as a lathe shape revolved around the Z-axis, with a profile curve going from the base radius up through the dome bulge and closing back along the axis at the top — representing a convex glass dome bulging out of the front face to show the stacked records inside.

I'm working out the dome profile curve with the arc sampled from top to base, closing it back along the axis. For the glass look I'm considering a paint shader with a dark teal tint and a diagonal sheen streak for a glassy reflection, but I need to figure out how to keep the records visible through it—maybe the dome should be an open shell rather than a fully closed, opaque surface.

Since the lathe wraps fully around the axis, the dome's apex faces the viewer directly along +Z, which means the apex itself needs to be the opening for the records to be visible — otherwise the solid cap would just block the view entirely.

I'm now working out how the records themselves should be oriented and stacked inside that dome opening so they read visually as a jukebox record stack rather than flat discs or coins, considering whether their edges or faces should point toward the viewer.

Actually, simpler: cut the dome apex off to form a porthole-like bezel opening, so the stack of records sits visible inside like looking through a window. Since the lathe surface only renders front-facing, the dome's inner shell won't block the view from the front through the hole, so the records stack will read clearly through the opening.

I'm now sketching the head geometry overall: placing the glowing arch of tubes spanning roughly x=±0.22 with a semicircular top near y=1.58, and fitting the dome window inside it centered around y=1.30 with radius about 0.15, making sure it clears the inner tube offsets of the arch so it reads as nested inside the arch rather than overlapping it.

I'm settling on a triple-ring arch design — outer red, middle amber, inner teal tubes — each with thin tube radius, with the inner ring sized to comfortably frame the dome window with margin to spare. I'm also considering adding a dark extruded arch-shaped backboard panel behind the glowing tubes to give them better contrast, essentially extruding the arch silhouette into a navy slab that sits just behind the colored tube rings.

Working out the extrusion geometry: I'm placing the backboard at the head's front z-position, defining its outline as a rectangle with a rounded semicircular top in local coordinates, so the arch shape reads correctly when extruded forward with its face oriented toward the viewer.

I need to reconcile widths and depths — the head block should span roughly ±0.22 to ±0.25 in x with its front face around z=0.22, but the arch backboard currently sticks out wider than the head itself, so I'm narrowing the arch to ±0.20 and adjusting the concentric tube radii (0.205, 0.178, 0.152) so everything nests properly within the head silhouette.

Now I'm working out the head's rounded-top silhouette coordinates in the z-y plane, making sure the sloped top doesn't leave the arch backboard floating above the solid surface — so I'm flattening the top region of the silhouette and lowering the arch's center height to around 1.32 with outer radius 0.215, keeping its peak just under the head's flat top at 1.535.

I realize the arch's legs would dip down into the lower cabinet's protruding front face, since the cabinet front sticks out 0.05 past the head front — so I'm repositioning the arch bottom to align with the head's bottom edge at 1.14 and pulling the cabinet top down to 1.12, giving the arch straight legs of 0.18 before the curve starts. I'm also considering setting the head front slightly recessed from the cabinet front to create a subtle visible ledge, then moving on to work out the dome window's center position.

Now I'm figuring out how the record stack sits inside the dome — whether the discs lie flat with their edges facing the viewer, stacked along the vertical axis with roughly 7 records spaced for an 8cm-tall stack, or whether they'd look better standing on edge facing forward instead.

I'll settle on flat horizontal records stacked in a column, showing colored label faces and black vinyl edges, with a small picker arm pivoting in from the side to grip a record at the stack's edge.

I can use rod's bone option to bind arm parts to the picker joint by name, since sweep options accept a joint reference string that resolves correctly. Now I'm positioning the record stack inside the dome cavity, behind the cut opening where the shell becomes visible, around z 0.24-0.26.

Actually looking through the hole from the front, the records' flat faces would be visible since they sit forward of z=0.24, appearing as horizontal strips through the opening. I'm reconsidering a cleaner structure instead: a chrome rim lathe plus a dark interior disc, with the record stack showing through the cut-away apex, redefining the dome's angular cap from the base up to where it's trimmed.

Working out the cut angle geometry, I settle on a dome radius around 0.15-0.16 with the cut angle near 40-42°, giving a hole radius of about 0.1 so the stacked records peek through partially rather than fully. But this makes the dome base wider than the inner arch tube radius, so I'm adjusting the arch dimensions outward (outer, mid, and inner tube radii) to keep enough clearance between the dome and the arch structure.

Checking the vertical placement, I position the dome's center slightly below the arch's center so its top stays inside the arch opening while its base just touches the top of the cabinet, keeping the legs of the arch clear of the dome's sides by a small margin. The record stack itself gets placed at the head's front plane with disc radius smaller than the dome's base radius so it reads as a stack peeking through the dome's opening.

I'm now reasoning about whether the records are visible through the hole at the dome's apex: since the records' radius is smaller than the hole's radius and the records sit along the central axis, a viewer looking straight on through the opening should see them unobstructed, since the shell material near the apex has been cut away for that viewing cone while the solid shell farther out doesn't intrude on those sightlines.

Rather than adding a glass pane over the hole, which would just hide the records, I'll leave it open so it reads as a porthole-style window, maybe giving the dome shell itself a glossy paint treatment to suggest glass. Then I'm moving on to positioning the picker arm's pivot post at the side of the dome, around x = 0.16.

For the arm placement, I'm checking whether its pivot post at various x positions collides with the arch legs or dome bulge, since those occupy similar space. I'll simplify by making the arm an L-shaped rod with a pivot near the dome's right edge that runs horizontally above the stack top, then checking whether this position keeps it visible through the dome's hole or partially occluded by the shell at the hole's edges.

The dome shell geometry is close to vertical near its base, so I'm accepting some overlap as stylized rather than physically perfect. I'll move on from fine-tuning this and settle on the flat-disc record stack design, then start writing the lower cabinet section.

I'm planning the cabinet with a cream lacquer silhouette body, a separate chrome kick plinth at the base, and chrome trim rods along the top front edge, working out the width proportions between the kick, cabinet, and head sections so they nest cleanly.

Reusing the chrome paint across multiple small parts should be fine for the sheet bake even with many tube charts. For the speaker grille I'm designing a starburst pattern using radial angle slicing into alternating colored wedges centered on the panel, with a chrome ring accent.

I need to verify how the extrude's surface attribute feeds local x,y coordinates into the paint function as the `s` parameter, confirming it only applies when a Paint-based fill and surface flag are both present, including for beveled inset vertices. That should hold correctly at the grille's front face corners too.

For the speaker grille bezel, since extrude only supports a single outline rather than a frame with a hole, I'm layering two slabs instead: a slightly larger chrome rounded-rect slab behind, and a smaller grille panel slab in front that protrudes just enough to leave a visible chrome border. I'll need a rounded-rectangle outline helper with arced corners to generate the point lists for both extrusions, and I'm considering adding bevels for smoother edges. For the coin slot, I'm planning a small chrome plate extrusion with a dark slot cutout and an attached coin-return button.

I'm now laying out the selection panel: a cream rounded-rect plate centered around y=0.83 with subtle grain, sized to hold a 3-row by 4-column grid of title cards and buttons, where each row has a card strip above a protruding cylindrical button mounted on the panel face.

For the title cards, I'm picking twelve jukebox-style song titles like "ROCK ALL NITE," "TUTTI FRUTTI," and "PEGGY SUE," rendered as small SVG cards with cream paper backgrounds, red borders, and bold red uppercase text sized to fit each card, plus a coin slot plate positioned at the bottom-right of the panel.

I'm matching the card texture's aspect ratio to the physical plane dimensions, and giving each button a colored cap with a chrome ring base for a retro look. Now I'm thinking through how to add a chrome pinstripe detail along the cabinet's side panels.

For the head's paint job, I decide to use a normal-based approach instead of a chrome spear: faces pointing mostly upward get chrome, faces pointing forward get red lacquer, and the rest get cream, with smooth blending between the zones based on the surface normal.

I'm checking how normals work for the extrude geometry — since vertices aren't shared across triangles, computed vertex normals end up as flat per-face normals, giving crisp creases between chart regions rather than smooth gradients, except at beveled edges where intermediate angles will naturally blend colors via the smoothstep threshold. That should work well for the sides and rim.

Now I'm moving on to color the three arch tube sweeps.

I'm leaning toward three concentric arches in distinct solid colors — red, amber, teal — at slightly different radii rather than banding colors along a single sweep, since that gives the cleanest "three tubes" look without extra mesh cuts from color transitions.

For the glow effect, I'm considering a paint function that brightens each tube's front-facing surface (where the normal points toward the viewer) by mixing the base color with white, creating a highlighted core that darkens toward the sides — giving a neon-lit appearance without needing a separate translucent halo layer.

Now I'm figuring out the arch backboard structure: a dark navy extrusion sitting in front of a slightly larger chrome rim extrusion to create a visible chrome border, with the glowing tubes mounted in front of that stack. I'm defining a general arch-outline function that traces up one side, arcs across the top with sampled points, down the other side, and closes along the bottom to form a single clean loop.

For the tubes, I'm sampling arch points at a given radius and smoothing them into a catmull-rom path for the sweep geometry, checking spacing so the inner tube arch doesn't collide with the dome's base — leaving just enough clearance between the dome radius and the tube radius while I settle on the dome's vertical center offset.

Reconsidering the dome: rather than lathing a solid cap (which risks closing into an awkward chord-shaped bezel), I decide a partial SphereGeometry band is cleaner — computing the sphere's radius and center so the band spans from a hole angle to a base angle, giving an open dome shell with a hole at the apex through which the record stack is visible. I work out the geometry so the base rim sits at the cabinet's front face and the hole rim sits slightly forward, then add thin chrome torus rings at both the base and hole edges for a bezel look, oriented so their default facing already points outward along +Z. Finally I plan the record stack behind the hole — thin horizontal cylinder discs stacked along Y — but realize that viewed from the front their edges are nearly invisible slivers, so I start considering reorienting the stack to read better through the hole.

For the records themselves, I settle on keeping them horizontal but giving each a paint function that colors the top cap differently near the center (a label color) versus the outer vinyl, using distance from the disc's own center computed in the paint closure, plus a faint groove pattern via a sine ripple on that radial distance. Each record needs its own paint instance since the label color differs, and I plan their stacked Y positions so a few are visible through the dome's hole from above.

Now I'm working out the picker arm mechanism — a small pivot joint mounted near the dome, with a rod extending to a gripper that holds a record, positioning it so it sits mostly within the hole region rather than clipping through the solid chrome band, since a pivot placed under the band would visually intersect the shell.

I decide to keep the arm simple: a pivot boss, a rod, and a gripper block, rigged under a dedicated "picker" bone separate from the main cabinet joint so it could be posed independently, though I'll leave it in a resting, unposed position for now. I also rough out remaining cabinet details — a coin slot painted onto a small plate with a dark rectangular slot region and a coin-return knob, plus confirming the starburst speaker grille and selector buttons are already planned.

I'm defining a chrome paint helper that brightens with the upward-facing normal component and darkens near grazing angles to fake a horizon reflection line, with a slight cool tint and subtle streak variation, making sure the return type is a proper RGB tuple. I also sketch a lacquer paint helper that blends body, front, and chrome-top colors using smoothstep thresholds on the normal's z and y components via the package's color-mixing utility, double-checking that the exported `mix` resolves to the paint-blending version rather than the bone-weight one.

I confirm the paint and extrusion-surface helpers I need (smoothstep, mix, noise-type functions) are all available from the package, and settle the joint hierarchy: a root "cabinet" joint at the origin, plus a secondary "picker" joint positioned at the arm's pivot with its local axis aimed leftward, while all other parts attach implicitly to the cabinet joint by proximity. Now I'm starting to pin down the actual numeric constants for the model's coordinates.

Now I'm working out the cabinet's side-profile silhouette as a set of z,y points, plus a separate chrome plinth profile at the base, figuring out appropriate inset/outset so the plinth reads as recessed trim rather than flush with the body
